text:
Droit de la famille — 151954

2015 QCCS 3717

SUPERIOR COURT

(Family Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

N
o
:

500-12-326305-152

DATE :

August 5,

2015

IN THE PRESENCE OF: THE HONOURABLE
CATHERINE MANDEVILLE, J.S.C.

S. K.

Plaintiff

c.

B. S. ET AL

Defendant

REVISED TRANSCRIPT OF REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

RENDERED ORALLY
ON JULY 16,

2015

______________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

JM-2307

[
1
]

The
Plaintiff
(Mrs. K.) has served the Defendant (Mr. S.) with
a Petition for divorce on April 15, 2015. She is now requesting that this Court
issue an Order dismissing all of Defendant’s proceedings and an Order for
Foreclosure based on
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
because Defendant
withholds, without valid ground, his consent to grant the ghet (Jewish
divorce).

[
2
]

More specifically,
Plaintiff
asked this Court :

-      to dismiss Defendant’s Motions to Quash
Seizures Before Judgment :

-

to strike Defendant’s detailed affidavits filed
in the present divorce file and those filed in support of the motions to quash
the seizures which he has filed as president of various corporate entities;

-

to strike all expert reports filed by the
Defendant;

-

to strike Defendant’s Introductive Motion for
Separation as to Bed and Board;

-

to foreclose him from filing any further
proceedings;

-

to authorize the
Plaintiff
to proceed to obtain
judgment against the Defendant in the divorce proceedings on an
ex parte

basis.

[
3
]

Defendant on his part presents a Motion for Interim orders
which concerns access to his children and a request to allow nesting, i.e. an
arrangement whereby the parents will alternate use of the parties’ residences
in accordance with their respective custodial rights.

CONTEXT

The
parties

[
4
]

The parties are observant Orthodox Jews who had a civil
marriage in New York on November 28, 2002 which was followed by a religious
marriage ceremony on March 12, 2003. They are both approximately 31 year old.

[
5
]

They are the parents of three children, two girls respectively
9 and 11 years old and a son who is 6.

Procedural
context

THE PLAINTIFF

[
6
]

The
Plaintiff
has filed for divorce on April 15, 2015. She has
also asked for interim measures and safeguard orders and a period of one day
has been set on August 24, 2015 for the hearing of these interim measures which
essentially concern the rights of the children (custody and/or access and child
support) as well as the use of domicile and secondary domicile, the spousal
support, provision for costs and household expenses.

[
7
]

After having served the Defendant with a Notice to remove all
the barriers to her remarriage (a request that Defendant be present before the
Rabbinical Tribunal to consent to the ghet) and having filed an affidavit in
conformity with
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
whereby she confirms
that her request has been sent in writing to Defendant and that he fails to
remove all barriers referred to in that request, the Plaintiff has now asked
this Court to use its discretion under section 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
to
dismiss all proceedings
[1]
by the Defendant, and foreclose him from any further proceedings.

[
8
]

The
Plaintiff
has also filed several motions to seize a number
of assets she claims belongs to the Defendant or are being used by the
Defendant for his personal benefit, although they belong to corporate entities
in which she claims to have rights, either through family patrimony or
matrimonial regime.

[
9
]

Finally, she has filed a Motion under section 54.1 C.c.p. in
another file, which pertains to Defendant’s request for separation as to bed
and board, asserting that such a motion for separation should be dismissed as
it constitutes an improper and abusive use of proceedings by the Defendant.

THE DEFENDANT

[
10
]

On his part, the Defendant has filed in the
divorce file a Motion for Interim and Safeguard Orders which relates to
custody, access and nesting. He has filed motions to quash the various seizures
and on last July 2, 2015, an Introductive Motion for Separation as to Bed and
Board (court file # 500-04-066333-155).

The
affidavit of the parties under
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act

[
11
]

After receiving the affidavit from
Plaintiff

dated April 28, 2015, the Defendant has, on May 1 2015, served a motion in the
divorce file for provisional measures and safeguard orders. This motion was
supported by a 73 paragraph detailed affidavit whereby he declares that he is
willing to consent to the ghet but that he truly desires reconciliation with
the Plaintiff.

[
12
]

Although no affidavit subscribed by the
Defendant was filed to specifically respond within the 15 days delay provided
for by
section 21.1 (4)
a) of the
Divorce Act
to the Plaintiff’s
affidavit under this section, there are several mentions in the affidavits that
the Defendant has filed in the court record, to which I will refer hereunder
specifically, whereby he indicates what are the genuine grounds for which he
has failed to consent to remove all barriers to the remarriage of the
Plaintiff.

[
13
]

Specifically the Defendant has stated the
following.  In his affidavit of reply to
Plaintiff
’s affidavit served on May
15, 2015, he states at paragraph 35 that:

35.

With respect to
paragraphs 63, 64 and 65, I truly believe that I, as a Jew and a father,
have
a moral and religious obligation to do everything possible
in order to keep
the family intact
and seriously consider reconciliation
for the benefit
of my children.

(Our emphasis)

[
14
]

Then in his responding affidavit to
Plaintiff
’s
motion to dismiss Defendant’s proceedings and for an order of foreclosure he
states at paragraph 8 that
:

8.

[...] I verily believe
that given the duration of our marriage and that three (3) children were born
issue of this marriage, that
it is our obligation from both a religious
perspective, as well as a community perspective, to pursue every avenue in
order to repair this marriage
;

9.

THAT it appears to me
however that
given the Motion to Dismiss, I may be denied my rights on an
interim and provisional basis, as well as a final judgment to maintain my
relationship with my children
;

[…]

11.

THAT I
may also be
deprived of my right to properly expose my financial situation
such that an
appropriate order will be rendered with respect to my financial obligations to
my family;

12.

THAT
I cannot accept

that my children will be deprived of my ongoing love, care and attention and
that
the Court may possibly dismiss my proceedings on its face
, given my
wife’s allegation that I refused to grant a religious divorce and
thus
should be precluded from exercising my legal recourses
;

13.

THAT
accordingly
,
in view of the above,
I undertake to attend at a reasonable date

scheduled,
to present myself before the Beth Din
in Montreal located at
6825 Decarie Blvd., Suite 100, in order that the rabbinical authorities deal
with this matter;

14.

THAT
I have no
alternative but to agree to a religious divorce in order to exercise my rights
before the Superior Court
.

(Our emphasis)

[
15
]

In his Motion introducing an action for
separation as to bed and board, the Defendant states :

Grounds
for Separation

21.

THAT the
parties
have been living separate and apart since April 15, 2015
and Defendant’s
will
to live together has been gravely undermined
in that :

a)

Defendant introduced
divorce proceedings and at the time of the application for separation, the
spouses are living apart;

b)

THAT
parties are at
an impasse with respect to their religious beliefs and practices
and
Plaintiff

recognizes that the parties need professional intervention in order to
determine whether any reconciliation is possible
.

(Our emphasis)

[
16
]

He further adds in this motion for separation
that the
Plaintiff
, Mrs K.,
has curtailed his contact with his children,
without valid reason
and that
he has attempted to communicate with her
in order to share custody without success
. He seeks urgent intervention
from the court as he fears for the well-being of his children in view of what
he calls Plaintiff’s “unilateral decisions” concerning the children. He adds in a detailed affidavit that at this point in time, “negotiations with Plaintiff
are
fruitless
” and that it is
therefore urgent that the Court intervenes in order to protect the well-being
of the children.

Proceedings
presented before this Court on July 8 and 9, 2015

[
17
]

Since the record already comprises a multitude
of proceedings, despite the Introductive Motion having been filed a mere three
months ago, it should be mentioned that the proceedings the Court was seized
with last July, 8 2015 are strictly those that were set to be heard on that
date by Justices Bénard and Hallée. They consist of the request by the

Plaintiff
for dismissal of Defendant’s proceeding and Order of foreclosure as
well as the Defendant’s Motion for Safeguard Oder and measures in the divorce
file (access rights).

THE
APPLICABLE LAW

[
18
]

Section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
which
forms the basis of the Plaintiff’s motion reads as follows :

21.(1)  In this section,

“spouse”

has the meaning assigned by subsection 2(1)
and includes a former spouse.

(2) In any proceedings under this Act, a spouse (in this section
referred to as the “deponent”) may serve on the other spouse and file with the
court an affidavit indicating

(
a
) that the other spouse is the spouse of the
deponent;

(
b
) the date and place of the marriage, and the
official character of the person who solemnized the marriage;

(
c
) the nature of any barriers to the remarriage of
the deponent within the deponent’s religion the removal of which is within the
other spouse’s control;

(
d
) where there are any barriers to the remarriage
of the other spouse within the other spouse’s religion the removal of which is
within the deponent’s control, that the deponent

(i) has removed those barriers, and the date and circumstances of
that removal, or

(ii) has signified a willingness to remove those barriers, and the
date and circumstances of that signification;

(
e
) that the deponent has, in writing, requested
the other spouse to remove all of the barriers to the remarriage of the
deponent within the deponent’s religion the removal of which is within the
other spouse’s control;

(
f
) the date of the request described in paragraph
(
e
);
and

(
g
) that the other spouse, despite the request
described in paragraph (
e
), has failed to remove all of the barriers
referred to in that paragraph.

Marginal note:
Powers of court where barriers not removed

(3) Where a spouse who has been served with an affidavit under
subsection (2) does not

(
a
) within fifteen days after that affidavit is
filed with the court or within such longer period as the court allows, serve on
the deponent and file with the court an affidavit indicating that all of the
barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(
e
) have been removed, and

(
b
) satisfy the court, in any additional manner
that the court may require, that all of the barriers referred to in paragraph
(2)(
e
) have been removed,

the court may, subject to any terms that the court considers
appropriate,

(
c
) dismiss any application filed by that spouse
under this Act, and

(
d
) strike out any other pleadings and affidavits
filed by that spouse under this Act.

Marginal note:
Special case

(4) Without limiting the generality of the court’s discretion
under subsection (3), the court may refuse to exercise its powers under
paragraphs (3)(
c
) and (
d
) where a spouse who has been served with
an affidavit under subsection (2)

(
a
) within fifteen days after that affidavit is
filed with the court or within such longer period as the court allows, serves on
the deponent and files with the court an affidavit indicating genuine grounds
of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers
referred to in paragraph (2)(
e
); and

(
b
) satisfies the court, in any additional manner
that the court may require, that the spouse has genuine grounds of a religious
or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers referred to in
paragraph (2)(
e
).

Marginal note:
Affidavits

(5) For the purposes of this section, an affidavit filed with the
court by a spouse must, in order to be valid, indicate the date on which it was
served on the other spouse.

Marginal note:
Where section does not apply

(6) This section does not apply where the power to remove the
barrier to religious remarriage lies with a religious body or official.

[
19
]

In
Bruker

vs
Marcovitz
[2]
, Justice Abella speaking for the Supreme
court explains the objective of this section and why it was adopted by the
Legislator. She specifically refers to the Minister’s words at the second
reading and to the reading of the amendments as made by the then Minister of
Justice , Mrs. Kim Campbell :

[5]
For an observant Jewish woman in Canada, this presents
a dichotomous scenario: under Canadian law, she is free to divorce her husband
regardless of his consent; under Jewish law, however, she remains married to
him unless he gives his consent. This means that while she can remarry under
Canadian law, she is prevented from remarrying in accordance with her religion.
The inability to do so, for many Jewish women, results in the loss of their
ability to remarry at all.

[7]        In response to these concerns,
after consultation with the leaders of 50 religious groups in Canada and with
the specific agreement of the Roman Catholic, Presbyterian and Anglican
churches, in 1990 the then Minister of Justice, Doug Lewis, introduced
amendments to the
Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp
.), Bill C-61, giving
a court discretionary authority to prevent a spouse from obtaining relief under
the Act if that spouse refused to remove a barrier to religious remarriage (
s.
21.1
).  At second reading, the Minister outlined the motivation for these
amendments, explaining:

The bill before us today is an amendment to the
Divorce Act
which would
provide a court with discretionary powers to preclude a spouse from obtaining
relief or proceeding under the Divorce Act where that spouse refuses to remove
a barrier to religious remarriage and where the power to remove the barrier to
religious remarriage lies solely with that person.  Where the court is
satisfied that the spouse who refuses to remove the barrier has genuine grounds
of a religious or conscientious nature for doing so, it need not exercise its
discretion to grant the remedy provided for in this legislation.

[…]  A spouse should not be able to refuse to participate in a Jewish
religious divorce — called a Get — in order to obtain concessions in a civil
divorce.  The Get should not be used as a bargaining tool for child
custody and access or monetary support.

[…]  I am concerned about protecting the integrity of the
Divorce Act

and preventing persons from avoiding the application of the principles
contained in the act.  For example, a wife may feel compelled to agree to
custody arrangements which are not truly in the best interests of a couple’s
child in order to obtain a Get.

I want to take a few minutes to describe briefly the dilemma certain
Jewish persons face because of their religious divorce procedures.  In the
Jewish religion divorce is accomplished by the delivery of a Get from the
husband and its acceptance by the wife in the presence of a Rabbinical
Court.  According to the Jewish religious traditions, the procedure cannot
be changed.  Without a Get, a Jewish woman cannot remarry in her own
faith.  Children of a subsequent civil marriage suffer religious
disabilities.  While difficult remarriage within the Jewish faith for a
man in the same circumstances is not impossible.

[...]

[...] the government is moving where it can and where it is brought to
the government’s attention to eliminate sexism and gender bias in the law. . .
.

[...]

It is the case that in some religions, the Roman Catholic, Greek
Orthodox and Islam, annulment or divorce may proceed more easily and faster if
the couple agree.

However, in all these cases, the authority to grant the annulment or
divorce rests with the religious tribunal, not the couple.

An un-co-operative spouse may delay a decision, but ultimately he or
she cannot prevent the religious tribunal from rendering its decision.

In these religions, the spouse initiating the action can ask the
religious authorities to deal with this problem.

The Jewish spouse does not have that recourse.

(
House of Commons Debates
, vol. VI, 2nd Sess., 34th Parl.,
February 15, 1990, at pp. 8375-77)

[8]        At third reading of these amendments, Kim Campbell, who
succeeded Mr. Lewis as Minister of Justice, confirmed the policy rationale for
this legislative initiative:

The purpose of this bill is to assist Jewish citizens whose spouses are
withholding a religious divorce, which is called a get, in order to obtain
concessions in a civil divorce. [...]

The consequences to women deprived of a get and loyal to their faith
are severe. They may not remarry within their faith, even though civilly
divorced. If they do remarry, children from a second civil marriage are
considered illegitimate and restricted from practising their religion. Such
consequences to a religious person leave them open to blackmail from the spouse
withholding the get.  For example, the spouse could say, “Give up your
claim for support or custody of the children and I will offer the get.” Even
those not contemplating a second marriage find it uncomfortable to be
considered married within their religion to someone they have divorced civilly.

The vast majority of adherents to the Jewish faith condemn as unfair
this practice of bargaining with the get.  Yet they are powerless to amend
the situation. Persuasion by rabbis has often proved ineffective.  Since
the dispersion of the Jews there is no central Jewish authority to amend the
Jewish legal code, [...] which governs the get. Nor is there any modern-day
authority within rabbinical courts to enforce the offer and receipt of gets.
Full support for Bill C-61 was expressed by major Jewish organizations who
attended the hearings before the legislative committee. Representatives of the
three Parties praised the bill and quickly passed two minor technical
amendments.

As well, the Toronto Board of Orthodox Rabbis [...] endorsed the
legislation and the two amendments.

[…]

[
Translation
]

Bill C-61 will enable Canada’s Jewish community to preserve its traditions
without destabilizing models of family life. It also ensures that the
principles of the
Divorce Act
with respect to alimony and custody are applied
equally to all Canadians.

(
House of Commons Debates
, vol. VIII, 2nd Sess., 34th Parl., May
4, 1990, at pp. 11033-34)

[9]        For many years, civil courts have attempted to remedy,
or compensate for, the husband’s recalcitrance in refusing to provide a
get
to
his wife.
They are often faced with assertions by the husband that
such interventions are a violation of his freedom of religion
.

[…]

[81]
Section
21.1
of the
Divorce Act
, which gives a court discretionary authority
to rebuff a spouse in civil proceedings who obstructs religious remarriage, is
a clear indication that it is public policy in this country that such barriers
are to be discouraged
.  As the comments of the then Ministers of
Justice show, these amendments received overwhelming support from the Jewish
community, including its more religious elements,
reflecting a consensus
that the refusal to provide a get was an unwarranted indignity imposed on
Jewish women and, to the extent possible, one that should not be countenanced
by Canada’s legal system
.

[82]
We also accept the right of Canadians to decide
for themselves whether their marriage has irretrievably broken down and we
attempt to facilitate, rather than impede, their ability to continue their
lives, including with new families. Moreover, under Canadian law, marriage and
divorce are available equally to men and women.  A get, on the other hand,
can only be given under Jewish law by a husband
.  For those Jewish
women whose religious principles prevent them from considering remarriage
unless they are able to do so in accordance with Jewish law, the denial of a
get is the denial of the right to remarry.  It is true that  get also
requires the consent of the wife, but as Ayelet Shachar points out in
Multicultural Jurisdictions, the law has a disparate impact on women:

The family
law realm […] vividly illustrates the troubling paradox of multicultural
vulnerability, by demonstrating how well-meaning attempts to respect
differences often translate into a license for subordination of a particular
category of group members — in this instance, primarily women. [p. 62]

The
refusal of a husband to provide a get, therefore, arbitrarily denies his wife
access to a remedy she independently has under Canadian law and denies her the
ability to remarry and get on with her life in accordance with her religious
beliefs
.

[…]

(Our emphasis)

[
20
]

The Court finds that these comments from the
various ministers are quite helpful to understand what are the objectives of
the law and how the discretion it provides the courts should be exercised.

[
21
]

To illustrate further the objective of this
section, this Court also wishes to refer to the case of
A.D.
v.
J.P.
[3]
which cites the Droit de la famille
québécois, CCH:

Ces changements, demandés par la communauté juive, ont pour but
d’éviter que
le refus d’accepter ou d’accorder un divorce religieux serve
d’outil de marchandage en vue d’obtenir des concessions en matière de garde,
d’accès ou d’aliments
.

(Our emphasis)

[
22
]

Essentially, all the authorities support the
proposition that the legislation granted the courts discretion to intervene
where a person withholds consent to give or receive the ghet, because this
person may use the ghet as a threat, a leverage tool or a negotiation tool with
the effect  that the other spouse who cannot obtain the religious divorce is
not able to freely address the Court and advance her rights as she or he
wishes.

[
23
]

Finally, the purpose of the use of the
discretion under
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
is very well described
by Justice Tannenbaum
[4]
:

The
Rabbinical court
cannot grant the ghet unless the husband consents, if the wife is the party
requesting the religious divorce.

It is not too difficult to imagine that the above situation has, over
the years, led to may instances where the threat of withholding consent,
has
forced many women into accepting unfair agreements with respect to either
custody, access, or financial arrangements in the civil divorce
.

With respect to people of the Jewish faith, who are divorcing,
section
21.1
of the

Divorce Act
is a way of levelling the playing
field.
The Jewish husband who threatens to withhold consent is subject to
being denied the right to petition for corollary relief or even a civil divorce
itself.

(Our emphasis)

Position
of the parties

THE PLAINTIFF

[
24
]

The
Plaintiff
, who describes herself as an
observant Satmar Jew, claims that all proceedings filed by the Defendant should
be dismissed and that he should be foreclosed from filing further proceedings
in any file because he uses his refusal to willingly consent to the ghet as a
threat and in order to obtain concessions from her in the civil proceedings
[5]
.

[
25
]

The
Plaintiff
’s position is that since she has
fulfilled her obligation to file an affidavit in conformity with
section 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
and since Defendant has failed to remove all the
barriers to her remarriage within her religion and has no genuine grounds of a
religious or conscientious nature to support his refusal, then the Court should
exercise its discretion to grant her motion.

[
26
]

She further explains that without a ghet she is
not only unable to remarry in her faith, but she is not even allowed to be
alone in the company of men and that she will continue, even if the civil
divorce were to be granted, to be seen in her community as an “agunah”, a woman chained to a dead marriage, who
has to maintain and respect all aspects of religious behaviour of a married
wife notwithstanding the civil divorce.

[
27
]

Furthermore, the
Plaintiff
claims that the
refusal of the Defendant to grant her the religious divorce (the ghet) on the
grounds that he wants a “reconciliation”, is false, since there is no
possibility of reconciliation (a fact that she has repetitively stated because
she does not want herself to reconcile) and that this allegation about
reconciliation is only made for the purpose of having an advantage or gaining
bargaining power in the civil divorce proceedings.

[
28
]

In other words, the
Plaintiff
claims that the
Defendant is using his power under religious law to refuse the ghet, for the
purpose of gaining advantage over her, which places her in the exact position
provision 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
was adopted to correct.  If she wants
to fully advance her rights before the civil courts without the impediment of a
threat of not obtaining the ghet and the inconveniences of living as an
“agunah”, she needs the Court to intervene.

THE DEFENDANT

[
29
]

The position of the Defendant is rather as
follows.  He claims that the
Plaintiff
does not have a right to obtain a ghet,
“
at this time
”, and that
there is no urgency for her to obtain it.

[
30
]

He highlights that the parties have been
separated for a mere two months
[6]
, and that he has “
a religious and community obligation to pursue
every avenue in order to repair the marriage
”.

[
31
]

To this effect, he has filed an expert “opinion” from Rabbi Reuben J. Poupko
[7]
who declares that in Jewish religious law and life, “it is
understood that the family is a singular bedrock of Jewish life” and who confirms that counselling and
reconciliation should be attempted by a couple before it seeks to obtain the
ghet. With respect to the evolution of civil proceedings versus the request for
ghet before the Rabbinical Tribunal, Rabbi Poupko goes on to state “
it is
not unusual for the ghet proceedings to go hand in hand with the civil
proceedings and conclude within a similar timeframe.
”
[8]

[
32
]

Consequently, the Defendant claims that he is
not refusing to consent to the ghet, but rather that he has genuine grounds of
a religious and conscientious nature for refusing to consent to the ghet
at
the present time
, in that he has the duty to protect family life and to
attempt reconciliation.

[
33
]

Defendant states that he is willing to consent
to a ghet but only in order to protect his relationship with his children and
his right to exercise his civil rights.

[
34
]

Defendant argues that
Plaintiff
’s Motion to
Dismiss and for Foreclosure is akin to an injunction or a safeguard order and
asks that the Court analyse the opportunity to grant Plaintiff’s motion in
accordance with the criteria that have to be present to issue such order,
being: urgency, appearance of right, the risk of a serious and irreparable
prejudice and the balance of convenience.

ANALYSIS

Absence of
urgency to obtain ghet

[
35
]

This Court disagrees with Defendant’s position
that the Motion to Dismiss Proceedings and to foreclose him from further
proceedings should meet the criteria of a Safeguard Order, including that of
urgency for the followings reasons.

[
36
]

First, there is no such criteria of urgency
provided for in
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
. Rather, the very short
delay of 15 days that is granted to a Defendant to respond to the affidavit of
the Plaintiff and to provide the Court with either a confirmation that all
barriers to religious remarriage have been removed or to satisfy the Court that
he has genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature to withhold
consent rather leads to conclude that this motion, without constituting an
urgency, should be dealt with efficiency.

[
37
]

Awaiting for the resolution of the civil
proceedings or even for the provisional measures to be decided and adopted
would go against the philosophy underlying
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act

which is that the Court may use its discretion to, as Justice Tannebaum so
rightly describes it
[9]
“
Level the playing fields
” in civil proceedings. Facing a similar argument to that raised by
the Defendant, Justice Tannenbaum states:

His willingness –
in that case, monsieur’s willingness
- to
grant the “Ghet” only after the civil divorce is completed leads me to conclude
that it is his intention to use his power over his wife in settlement
negotiations.  His offer to consent to the “Ghet” after the civil divorce is
meaningless since he would, in no way, be bound to do so.
Section 21.1
, in my
view, clearly indicates
that the barriers are to be removed prior to the
completion of the civil proceedings, since it empowers the Court to dismiss any
proceedings taken by the refusing spouse
.

On the other hand, agreeing to the “Ghet” prior to
completion of the civil divorce would, in no way, prevent the husband from continuing
with his proceedings, including his request for custody and the compensatory
allowance
, etc. and
therefore letting the Court decide on these matters based on any evidence that
he may tender.

(Our emphasis)

[
38
]

The courts have repeatedly determined in similar
situations where it was argued that the civil proceedings should be resolved
before the ghet needed to be granted, that it would be useless to wait after
the civil proceedings are resolved since no court can force a party to grant or
accept the ghet as only the Rabbinical Court can grant it after it is satisfied
it has been validly given and validly received.

[
39
]

Since the purpose of
section 21.1
of the
Divorce
Act
is to level the playfield and allow a party to advance his or her
rights without fearing the threat of the possibility that the ghet will not
eventually be granted, this Court is of the opinion that if it is in the
presence of such a threat and is not satisfied that the ghet is refused for
genuine religious or conscientious grounds, then it should exercise its
discretion at any time after the divorce motion is filed.

[
40
]

Such also appears to be the position adopted by
the courts, notably in the decision rendered by Justice Tannebaum referred to
above and in the case of
Darel
v.
Darel
[10]
, a
case rendered by the Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta, which has decided at
paragraph 50:

Where the c
ourt is of the view that it would be
inappropriate to lend its support to a litigant who has improperly withheld a
religious divorce, this would constitute a
preliminary objection
even to
the litigant bringing an application for modification of an existing judgment.

(Our emphasis)

[
41
]

Indeed, if we want to allow each party to
address the Court and advance his or her  rights without the undue pressure or
threat of a ghet refusal, it is necessary that a motion based on
section 21.1

Divorce
act

be treated as a preliminary objection and decided before the debate
takes place before the courts.

[
42
]

Furthermore the motion before this Court was not
filed as a request for injunctive measures or for an interim measure nor was it
treated as such by our courts. It was filed last May and was set to be heard
for 2 hours
[11]
. It was treated as an interlocutory motion.

[
43
]

Now turning to the Defendant’s argument based on
the expert opinion of Rabbi Poupko that civil proceedings and ghet proceedings
evolve hand in hand and that it is not uncommon that they resolve
simultaneously.

[
44
]

This Court has determined that the opinion of
Rabbi Poupko on that subject is not receivable as per the criteria of relevance
and necessity described by the Supreme Court in the case of
R
. vs
Mohan
[12]
and recently affirmed by the Supreme Court in
White Burgess
vs

Abbott and Haliburton
[13]
.

[
45
]

This Court is not applying Jewish religious law
and has no control over the Rabbinical Court. What it has, however, is full
jurisdiction under the
Divorce Act
and the
Code of civil procedure

to control procedure and decide any and all claims made under the
Divorce
Act
or claims for separation as to bed and board.

[
46
]

The opinion of a rabbi as to what is the status
of Jewish religious law is here of no assistance to the Court’s determination
of the issues at stake.The opinion of the rabbi as to how civil proceedings
should evolve is irrelevant because the Court is experienced in domestic law
and
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
certainly constitutes domestic law.

[
47
]

Turning now to another argument of the Defendant
whereby he asserts that the discretion of the Court to dismiss all proceedings
should be exercised with caution since it is of the same nature as the power to
dismiss abusive proceedings under section 54.1 of the
Code of Civil
Procedure
.

[
48
]

Although the
Court agrees that the objectives of these dispositions bear a resemblance, in
that they both aim to ensure that a party can address the Court and advance his
right without fear of the other party’s conduct,
section 21.1
of the
Divorce
Act
and section 54.1 of the
Code of Civil Procedure
differ greatly
in that under 54.1, it is the party seeking for the dismissal or other measures
who needs to show
prima facie
an abusive conduct and/or proceeding from
the other party.  Under section 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
, the Court may
use its discretion once it finds that the spouse who has been asked to remove
all barriers has not responded by an affidavit that such barriers have been
removed. It is up to that spouse to satisfy the Court either that he has
removed such barriers or that he has a genuine ground for not removing them.

[
49
]

This now brings us to the crucial issue at
stake, the determination of whether or not this Court should  use its
discretion under 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
to dismiss all proceedings and
foreclose the Defendant from further acting before it.

[
50
]

Defendant has not filed a specific affidavit
which would correspond to that described in section 21.1.3 a) of the
Divorce
Act
stating that all barriers refer in paragraph 2 have been removed,
neither has he, either in his affidavits or in his argument before the Court,
confirmed that such was the case.  Rather, he has declared in his affidavits on
file that he is willing to consent to a ghet in order to protect his
relationship with his children and his right to exercise his judicial rights.

[
51
]

This form of “willingness” to consent while
coerced to do so in order to protect his rights cannot amount to, as Defendant
knows and admits himself, a free and wilful consent which will enable the
Rabbinical tribunal to grant the ghet.

[
52
]

Indeed, as Defendant pleads it
[14]
, “
Plaintiff
is also well aware that a ghet cannot be obtained
without the free and enlighten consent of Defendant which is a non realistic
expectation for Plaintiff to have at the present time. Short of lying to the
Rabbinical Court, Defendant is without recourse”. Therefore, Defendant is fully
knowledgeable that what he states is his consent is not a genuine consent that
is valid to proceed before the Rabbinical Court.

[
53
]

A similar argument was raised before Justice
Décarie in Droit de la famille, 3558
[15]
,
who found that the fact that someone was saying he was willing to consent but
was felt coerced to consent in order to protect his right was not a valid
ground for refusing to remove all barriers.

[
54
]

The Defendant has not satisfied this Court that
he has performed what is necessary to remove all barriers to a religious
marriage.

[
55
]

This now brings us to the second issue in
debate, which is whether or not the Defendant has satisfied the Court that it
should refuse to exercise its discretion because his refusal to consent to the
removal of the barriers to remarriage is based on a genuine ground of a
religious or conscientious nature.

[
56
]

The essential expression   that has to be
considered is “
genuine ground
”.  This expression in the
Divorce Act

corresponds in the French version to “
un motif sérieux
”.

[
57
]

Defendant claims that it is his religious belief
and his conscientious belief that all attempts should be made at
reconciliation. When referring to reconciliation stemming from his religious
belief, Defendant again refers to the expert opinion of Rabbi Poupko, who
confirms that it is part of Jewish faith that couples should seek and make
every efforts and attempt reconciliation.

[
58
]

This Court does not doubt that Rabbi Poupko
could be considered an expert in Judaism or in religious Jewish law, but his
opinion is inadmissible, again as per
R.
vs
Mohan
, since his
opinion is not necessary to determine what this Court has to decide at this
stage of the proceedings.

[
59
]

Defendant claims that it is, in his religion and
conscience, a duty for him to attempt reconciliation.  The Court readily
accepts this affirmation that it forms part of his religion and also his
conscience.  In Civil law and it is likely the case in many religions,  the
parties have to consider reconciliation before introducing divorce proceedings.

[
60
]

Indeed, the
Divorce Act
specifically
states that a lawyer has to advise his client before entertaining divorce
proceedings about the provisions of the Divorce Act which have as their object
reconciliation and  to discuss the possibility of reconciliation .  This lawyer
( and eventually the court seized with the Divorce motion) has a duty to
ascertain that there is no possibility of reconciliation and also has to advise
his client that counselling may be available if the client wants to attempt
reconciliation.

[
61
]

Plaintiff
has specifically declared in her
Introductory Motion for Divorce that she has benefited from such counselling by
her lawyer and that she has been informed that reconciliation should be
entertained before divorce proceedings are filed. In spite of this advice, she
has maintained her decision to file for divorce.

[
62
]

It is not necessary for this Court to rely on
any expert opinion, to accept that reconciliation may, depending on the
circumstances, be a conscientious or a religious ground for refusing to consent
to the ghet.

[
63
]

Whether the Defendant has a “genuine” or a
“sérieux” ground in the present case is what is the crux of this matter.  To
determine this issue, the opinion of Rabbi Poupko is of no assistance.  He is
not Mr. S., cannot speak as to what is the Defendant’s subjective belief under
his conscience and he cannot help the Court determine whether or not, in this
case, this belief is genuine or not.

[
64
]

The assessments of the genuine character of the
ground can be made by, amongst other means, verifying whether the ground is
advanced by someone whose acts abide by this asserted religious belief and who
acts according to his conscientious belief. To be considered genuine, a belief,
be it religious or conscientious, should not only be words uttered to avoid the
consequences of the law, the ground should be authentic,  the true reflection
of this person’s state of mind and not be frivolous. It needs to have some
roots in reality.

[
65
]

Defendant’s ground for refusing to validly
consent to the ghet is that he feels compelled, in accordance with his
religious belief and his conscience, to reconcile with the
Plaintiff

at this
stage
.

[
66
]

The Court is not satisfied that this ground in
the Defendant’s case is genuine.  Defendant can certainly appreciate that
reconciliation is a process which, just as marriage, requires the agreement of
two people. One cannot force another to reconcile.  “At this stage”, as he
himself puts it, the
Plaintiff
is so convinced of the impossibility to
reconcile with the Defendant, that after attempting to save her marriage by
attending couple counselling, she has applied for divorce, notably, on the
basis of mental cruelty; mental cruelty of such a kind as to render
“intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses”.

[
67
]

Plaintiff
states in her multiple affidavits that
the Defendant has had an abusive conduct towards her which is why she has
decided to serve him with a motion for divorce. She further has adamantly
affirmed that there is no chance of reconciliation between the parties.

[
68
]

While the Court can appreciate that a spouse who
has just been served with the divorce proceeding may want to attempt
reconciliation, and while the law indeed imposes upon the attorney the duty to
have his client consider the possibility of reconciliation, it is abundantly
clear from the
Plaintiff
’s assertions that she wants nothing to do with it.
This absence of willingness of one of the spouses to attempt reconciliation
should put an end to any possibility of such a process taking place  between
the parties.

[
69
]

Defendant “at this stage”, knows the
Plaintiff
’s
position, he can no longer realistically claim that reconciliation is possible.
Moreover,  the number of proceedings that have been filed by both parties and
their content is quite indicative of a high level of animosity  which makes it
very unlikely that they would eventually overcome their differences.

[
70
]

Finally, and most importantly, the ground based
on reconciliation cannot seriously be construed as genuine once considered in
the light of the Defendant’s Motion for Separation as to Bed and Board.  His
position by filing such a motion is very contradictory to that which he
entertains as a serious ground or a genuine ground for opposing consent to the
ghet.

[
71
]

Indeed, Defendant’s application to obtain a
separation as to bed and board specifies that his wife’s will to live together
with him has been “
gravely undermined
” and that the “
parties are at
an impasse with respect to their religious beliefs and practices
”.

[
72
]

The very purpose of a motion for separation is
to have the Court declare that the parties are separated because their
willingness to live together has been gravely undermined. It should be further
stressed that
article 505
of the
Civil Code of Quebec
provides that a
reconciliation of the parties constitutes a “
fin de non-recevoir
” to the
separation as to bed and board.

[
73
]

It is difficult to see how Defendant’s position
that he wants reconciliation can be construed as genuine when just a few days
ago, on July 2 last, he opted to file a Motion for Separation as to Bed and
Board which has no chance of success if the parties are to reconcile.

[
74
]

In the divorce proceeding, Defendant states that
he wants to reconcile and he files a Motion for Shared Custody and for Nesting
and now, very recently, he files a Motion for Separation as to Bed and Board
whereby he again makes the same type of claim with respect to the children
(shared custody and nesting).

[
75
]

This convinces the Court that his refusal to
grant the ghet is not based on the genuine ground or belief that the parties
shall reconcile.  The Court finds it rather likely, based on Defendant’s manner
of acting in his proceedings, notably his decision to make the same demands
pertaining to the children in the Motion to Separate as to Bed and Board, that
he is trying to shield himself from a potential decision of the Court to dismiss
all of his proceedings and to foreclose him from making any further proceedings
under the
Divorce Act
.

[
76
]

Seeing that this Court considers the Defendant
has not satisfied his burden of showing that his refusal to remove all barriers
to the remarriage is based on a genuine ground of a religious or conscientious
nature and considering that this Court is of the view that the Defendant is
likely using his refusal to grant the ghet as means to gain an advantage over
the
Plaintiff
in the negotiation of the multiple issues (either of a financial
or a custodial nature) which will have to be resolved in the civil proceedings,
this Court will exercise its discretion and dismiss Defendant’s proceedings and
affidavits in the divorce file.

[
77
]

An argument was made by Defendant that by
dismissing all of the Defendant’s proceedings, the Court was unduly affecting
the children’s rights because a father advances the children’s rights when he
is requesting for either access or custody or nesting.

[
78
]

The Court wishes to mention that at the hearing
that took place on July 8 and July 9 last, it has expressed some concern, as
had justice Bénard previously, seeing that there were
no interim measures adopted yet in the present file which provided the children
with specific time with their father. However, the Court was reassured by the
evidence provided, that the children, indeed, have an opportunity to benefit
from regular and appropriate contact with their father at the present time.

[
79
]

As previously mentioned, the objective of

section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
is specifically to preclude access to the Court to a spouse who,
without justification, refuses to consent to the ghet and will likely use it to
gain an advantage or concessions not only for financial purposes but also on
issues pertaining to custody and access.

[
80
]

If Defendant acts in such a way that the ghet
cannot be granted, then it is him who makes the choice of precluding himself
from benefiting from the Court’s assistance.

[
81
]

Any court, just as this Court has done in the present instance, is bound to render
any decision that pertains to the children in consideration only of  their best
interest. Such is the law that the Superior Court will undoubtedly continue to
apply in the subsequent proceedings.

[
82
]

That being said, in view of the intensity of the
litigation between the parties, this Court believes it will be necessary to
have an order rendered for the benefit of the children so that they know the
boundaries of the access rights and understand the custodial situation, and
also, so that the order will be binding on both parties and enforceable.

[
83
]

A date has already been set to hear provisional
measures next August 24. At this date, the court will be seized with the issue
of custody and access and the modalities pertaining to same. If the court then
needs to obtain further information to identify the best interest of the
children it will be able to rely on several solutions even in the absence of
the Defendant. For example, a lawyer may be appointed for the children so that
they can voice what is their interest or there may be an order for a social
expertise to which the parties will collaborate.

[
84
]

Therefore, there is no need, at this point in
time, to issue provisional orders with respect to custody, accesses or nesting
since these issues will be properly dealt with by the Court on August 24, 2015.

[
85
]

There remains the request for dismissal of all
proceedings in the file of Separation as to Bed and Board.  As has been decided
already in several cases, there is no litispendance between a divorce and
separation as to bed and board because the finality of these motions is not the
same.  However, such a difference in finality may not be present when it comes
to accesses, custody or child support because then, a judge who sits and
presides the case be it in the Divorce file or the Separation file, will be
seized with exactly the same issues between the same parties and have the same
object
.
This is why in
several decisions and notably the case of
Gobeille
vs
Savard
[16]
,
it has been decided that, if orders
were to be rendered in the divorce file, these take precedence over those
rendered in the separation as to bed and board file.

[
86
]

The Court understands and is fully aware that
under the
Divorce Act
, it may dismiss or strike
any proceedings or affidavits and make orders of foreclosure for any
proceedings
under this Act
. Therefore, under 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
,
strictly speaking, the Court would not have the power to render a dismissal
order of proceedings or to strike proceedings in the file that relates to
separation as to bed and board because it is not a motion filed by the
Defendant under the
Divorce Act
.

[
87
]

However, for the purpose of rendering effective
the Court decision that is rendered under 21.1 of the
Divorce Act
, and
seeing its powers under articles 2, 20 and 46 of the
Code of Civil Procedure
,
this Court finds that it is necessary to use its power to suspend the
proceedings of separation as to bed and board.

[
88
]

Therefore, since the Code provides that a judge
may determine which proceedings will be examined first, and with a view of
rendering effective the orders amended under
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
,
this Court will suspend all proceedings in the file bearing number 500-04-066333-155, and these proceedings will be
suspended so long as the Defendant has not filed an affidavit confirming that
the ghet has been granted.

[
89
]

There have been several decisions whereby delays
have been granted to the spouse who was making obstruction, so as to  to leave
him time to remove all the barriers to remarriage. In a similar situation, the
Court of Appeal
[17]
suggested that perhaps an order providing the spouse with a
ultimate delay to remove obstacles should have been granted.

[
90
]

This Court believes, seeing the Defendant’s
position, that he was not ready “at this time” to give the ghet, that it should grant him a further delay, now
that he is aware of the Court’s decision, to take all the necessary
arrangements to obtain the ghet and to make sure that the ghet is indeed
obtained.

[
91
]

A delay will be granted up to August 21 because
on August 24 a hearing is set with respect to custody, accesses and other
measures and there will be interim orders rendered. Should the Defendant want
to participate in this debate and be authorized to do so, he shall prove to the
Court that all obstacles have been removed at the latest on August 21.

[
92
]

The
Plaintiff
asked that the affidavits of the
Defendant, including those  subscribed as an officer of a variety of corporate
entities be stricken from the record.
Section 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
does not allow the Court to dismiss the proceedings of a
person other than that who fails to remove the obstacles to remarriage.
Therefore this Court will not strike any proceedings that were filed by these
corporate entities, nor the affidavits supporting same because the Defendant
has not subscribed them personally but has rather made the declarations that
appear in those affidavits in his capacity of officer of a corporation.

[
93
]

Therefore, the affidavits this Court strikes
from the record are those personal to Mr. S., those filed to support his
own motions or to advance his personnal rights but not the affidavits that
support the various motions introduced by the corporate entities.

[
94
]

FOR THESE REASONS
,
this Court:

[
95
]

GRANTS
the

Plaintiff
’s Motion to dismiss the Defendant’s proceedings and personal
affidavits in the divorce file;

[
96
]

STRIKES
any and
all proceedings and affidavits of Defendant filed on his own behalf in the
divorce file;

[
97
]

FORECLOSES
the
Defendant to file into the divorce file any new proceeding;

[
98
]

AUTHORIZES
Defendant
to refile in this Court record his divorce proceedings at the latest on August
21, 2015 if, and only if, he files at the same time an affidavit indicating
that all the barriers to the
Plaintiff
’s remarriage in the Jewish faith have
been removed. Failing such an affidavit being filed, the Plaintiff will

thereafter

BE AUTHORIZED
to proceed
ex parte
;

[
99
]

SUSPENDS
all
proceedings in the file which concerns the Motion for Separation as to Bed and
Board (500-04-066333-155);

[
100
]
